title: Near-Total Lunar Eclipse to Create Blood Moon Visible Across Americas on August 28
excerpt: A deep partial lunar eclipse will cover 96% of the moon later this month, producing a striking red 'blood moon' effect visible across North and South America, Europe, and Africa — the best lunar eclipse until 2028.
body:
• A deep partial lunar eclipse on the night of August 27-28 will cover 96% of the moon's surface, creating a near-total "blood moon" visible across the Americas, Europe, and Africa.
  • The eclipse begins at 6:23 PM PT on August 27 and reaches maximum coverage at 9:12 PM PT, making it prime viewing time for West Coast observers.
  • This will be the most impressive lunar eclipse visible from the United States until a total lunar eclipse on December 31, 2028.
  • The event caps a remarkable August for skywatchers, coming just two weeks after the total solar eclipse that crossed Europe on August 12.

Two weeks after a total solar eclipse swept across Europe, skywatchers across the Americas are set for their own celestial spectacle: a near-total lunar eclipse on the night of August 27-28 that will turn the full moon a deep shade of red.

The partial lunar eclipse will see 96% of the moon pass into Earth's dark umbral shadow — so deep that it will produce what astronomers are calling an "almost blood moon." At maximum eclipse, only a sliver of the moon's edge will remain in direct sunlight, while the rest glows with the eerie copper-red hue characteristic of total lunar eclipses.

When and Where to Watch

The eclipse unfolds over about five and a half hours. For viewers on the West Coast, the penumbral phase begins at 6:23 PM PT on Wednesday, August 27, with the partial eclipse starting at 7:33 PM PT. The moon reaches maximum eclipse at 9:12 PM PT, making it ideal prime-time viewing. The partial phase ends at 10:51 PM PT, with the penumbral phase wrapping up just after midnight.

"Because this eclipse covers 96% rather than the full disk, astronomers have dubbed it an "almost blood moon" — though the visual effect will be striking."

On the East Coast, the timing is equally favorable: the partial eclipse begins at 10:33 PM ET on August 27, peaks at 12:12 AM ET on August 28, and concludes at 1:51 AM ET.

The eclipse will be visible across North America, South America, Europe, and Africa. According to Time and Date, about 987 million people — roughly 12% of the world's population — will be able to see all phases of the event, while around 1.3 billion will see the full partial phase. Western U.S. states, along with northern Chile and inland Brazil, statistically offer the best odds of clear skies.

Why It Turns Red

During a lunar eclipse, Earth blocks direct sunlight from reaching the moon. But the planet's atmosphere bends some sunlight around its edges, filtering out blue wavelengths and allowing red light to pass through and illuminate the lunar surface. The result is the distinctive "blood moon" effect. Because this eclipse covers 96% rather than the full disk, astronomers have dubbed it an "almost blood moon" — though the visual effect will be striking.

A Rare Opportunity

This will be the first deep partial lunar eclipse anywhere in the world since September 18, 2024. The next partial lunar eclipse, in January 2028, will cover just 2.4% of the moon's surface. That makes the August 2026 event the best lunar eclipse globally until a total lunar eclipse on New Year's Eve 2028 — more than two years away.

The event also coincides with August's full "Sturgeon Moon," named by Native Americans near the Great Lakes for the freshwater fish that were abundant in late summer. The name dates to a tradition of harvesting sturgeon — a species that can grow over six feet long and dates back 136 million years — during this time of year.

An August to Remember

August 2026 has been an exceptional month for astronomy. The total solar eclipse on August 12 brought totality to parts of Russia, Greenland, Iceland, and Spain, with a partial eclipse visible across Europe, Africa, and parts of North America — the first time totality reached mainland Europe since 1999. The peak of the Perseid meteor shower, one of the year's best, also fell on August 12.

No special equipment is needed to watch the lunar eclipse. Unlike solar eclipses, lunar eclipses are safe to view with the naked eye, and binoculars or a small telescope will enhance the experience. Clear skies and a location away from city lights will provide the best viewing conditions.
